title: The one-minute weather window: six bilingual weather phrases before breakfast
description: Stand at the same window each morning and decide together what the weather is doing, in the language you are building. Six phrases, one minute, no chart needed.
book_line: Bilingual English-Spanish vocabulary book for kids: themed word lists and simple activities, read on a Kindle, copied into a notebook when you want them on paper.
pin_title: The one-minute weather window: six bilingual weather phrases before breakfast
body:
Every morning somebody looks outside to decide what to wear. Do that with your child, at the same window, and you have a daily vocabulary moment that needs no materials at all.

Start with six phrases, choosing the ones your local weather actually produces: it's sunny (hace sol), it's raining (está lloviendo), it's cloudy (está nublado), it's cold (hace frío), it's hot (hace calor), it's windy (hace viento).

Ask the same question every morning, in the language you are building: "¿Qué tiempo hace?" — or "what's the weather like?". Your child looks and answers. At first they will copy yesterday's answer or just point at the sky; say the phrase for them and move on.

Once the phrases are familiar, add a follow-up that connects the weather to the day: "Hace frío. ¿Qué nos ponemos?" / "It's cold. What shall we put on?". Now the weather word leads straight into a decision, which is how it gets used.

On some days, let your child be the forecaster. They stand at the window and announce the weather to the family in the language you are building. A child announcing something to the room is speaking with confidence, even when the forecast is wrong.

You may notice that the Spanish phrases do not all follow one pattern: hace sol and hace frío, but está lloviendo and está nublado. There is no need to explain it. Say each phrase the same way every day, as a whole, and your child will pick it up as a whole.

A second week can add a little more: yesterday versus today. "Ayer llovió, hoy hace sol" / "yesterday it rained, today it's sunny". Keep it to one comparison; the window routine should stay a minute long.

What to skip: a weather chart. Charts are a nice idea that turns into one more thing to keep up. The window is already there, and the weather changes it for you.

And on mornings when nobody has time, one word is enough: "¡sol!" or "rain!". The habit matters more than the length.

Question and follow-up scripts in both directions. Grammar note limited to 'these are said as whole phrases' to avoid an inaccurate rule.
